title: Ramanand: where shall I go
hook: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love (Basant, Ramanand, ang 1195)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadhna's nadar: the lion and the jackal, the rainbird, the boat that comes too late. Your line was saved by grace. Where did you ask, or admit you needed help you couldn't earn? Day seven hundred eighty-six.

The bag is packed. The offering is ready: sandalwood, ground fine, mixed with sweet oils, the good stuff saved for a holy day. You're at the door, keys in hand, about to set out for the temple. And then you stop, and set the bag down, and don't go. Not out of laziness. Because something just became clear. Three days ago, Sain the barber named a teacher in his hymn: Ramanand, who knows the devotion of the Lord. Today Ramanand speaks for himself, and his hymn begins at that door.
screen: `SANDALWOOD READY, BAG PACKED.` → `AT THE DOOR, YOU STOP.` → `RAMANAND SPEAKS FOR HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Ramanand's hymn is in Raag Basant, the raag of spring, on Ang 1195. It opens with a question, in paraphrase: where shall I go? My own home is colored with love. My mind no longer wanders off; it has gone still. Then he tells how it happened. One day, he says, a longing rose up in me. I ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God at the holy place. And the Guru showed me that God within my own mind. The trip turned around at the door. Next comes a line with a gentle sting. Wherever I go, he sings, I find water and stone: bathing places and carved images. But You fill them all, equally. I've looked through the Vedas and the Puranas, the old scriptures. Go there, he says, only if He isn't here. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the temple is empty or the old books are worthless. He says the One who fills the temple fills the home too, and fills everything equally. So the long walk isn't needed to find what's already here. Then the close, in paraphrase: True Guru, I'm a sacrifice to You, who cut away all my confusion and doubt. Ramanand's Lord is the all-pervading One, and the Guru's Word cuts away countless deeds. Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher whose circle reached far, and some say Kabir learned from him. In the Granth, he leaves this one image: a house dyed with love, so full that there's nowhere else to go.
screen: `WHERE SHALL I GO? MY HOME IS COLORED.` · `SANDALWOOD READY, THE TRIP TURNS AROUND.` · `GO THERE ONLY IF HE ISN'T HERE.` · then, large: `THE GURU'S WORD CUTS THE DOUBT.`

segments.voice: The practice: stay home and pray, if you pray. If you don't, simply stay. Use the sit right where you are, in whatever room this is. Don't wish yourself somewhere holier. Notice the ordinary things around you: the wall, the light, the sounds from the next room or the street. Let this place be enough for two minutes. If the mind wants to pack a bag and go somewhere better, let it set the bag down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ramanand. The teacher Sain named, whose hymn in Raag Basant turns around at the door: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love?
Your line: colored at home. Today, the next time you think peace is somewhere else, look once around the room you're in first. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Ramanand's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Basant, and Sikh teaching speaks of finding the Lord within, guided by the Guru's Word.

original.note: Gurmukhi: color, dye, love; Ramanand's home is 'colored' with it (Ang 1195).

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn against going to temples.
what it means: the One who fills the temple fills the home equally, so there's nowhere else to go.
what a scholar hears: the turn comes through the Guru, who shows God within; the hymn closes on the Guru's Word.
recall: the one who cherishes the poor
the city where sorrow doesn't live

notes: Hymn paraphrased from memory (kat jaaeeai re ghar laago rang; ek divas man bhaee umang; so braham bataaio gur man hee maahi; jahaa jaaeeai tah jal pakhaan; bed puraan sabh dekhe joe, oohaan tau jaaeeai jau eehaa na hoe; ramanand suaamee raman braham; gur kaa sabad kaatai kot karam). 'Kot karam' is rendered 'countless deeds' to avoid a number. Please check.
'Water and stone' is glossed as bathing places and carved images; confirm the reading is fair and not dismissive of Hindu practice.
Kabir learning from Ramanand is stated as 'some say' (also marked as tradition in year one, day 252).
Basant as 'the raag of spring' is general background; confirm.
Editor: fixed the day count (Sain was day 783, three days back, not two).
